books.section: The United States as an Imperialist Power

primary_sources: Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890)
Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899
Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898
Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900
President William McKinley, proclamation on the Philippines, December 21, 1898

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which debates over imperialism changed American ideas about the nation's role in the world between 1890 and 1902.

documents.title: Mahan on sea power
documents.source: Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1890. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Mahan, a serving naval captain writing for naval officers and policymakers, arguing that sea power decides which nations matter. Paraphrased from the book.
documents.text: Mahan argued that a nation's greatness rests on sea power, which needs a strong navy, coaling stations, and overseas bases to protect trade. A nation that neglects its navy, he warned, will lose its markets and its standing among the great powers.

documents.title: "The White Man's Burden"
documents.source: Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Kipling, a British poet, writing for an American magazine in the month the Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris. The poem urges Americans to accept empire as a duty.
documents.text: Take up the White Man's burden — Send forth the best ye breed — Go bind your sons to exile To serve your captives' need; To wait in heavy harness, On fluttered folk and wild — Your new-caught, sullen peoples, Half-devil and half-child.

documents.title: "The March of the Flag"
documents.source: Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898. Public domain (abridged).
documents.sourcing: Beveridge, an Indiana Republican campaigning in 1898 — he was elected to the Senate in 1899 — speaking months before the Senate debated annexing the Philippines in January and February 1899. The speech argues empire is continuity with the founders.
documents.text: If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did — we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward — we only continue the march of the flag?

documents.title: McKinley's "benevolent assimilation"
documents.source: President William McKinley, proclamation on the Philippines, December 21, 1898. Paraphrased, with two short verbatim phrases.
documents.sourcing: McKinley, the president who decided to keep the Philippines, instructing American forces in the islands. A public statement of policy, not a private doubt.
documents.text: McKinley ordered American forces to extend American rule over the Philippines, calling the mission "benevolent assimilation" and saying the United States came "not as invaders or conquerors, but as friends, to protect the natives in their homes, in their employments, and in their personal and religious rights."

documents.title: Twain turns anti-imperialist
documents.source: Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Twain, a vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League, speaking to a newspaper in the middle of the 1900 election campaign. The passage shows a public change of mind.
documents.text: I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific. … But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. … And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land.

documents.title: The Anti-Imperialist League platform
documents.sourcing: The League, founded in 1898 to oppose annexing the Philippines, stating its platform for the public. Paraphrased from the platform.
documents.text: The League declared that ruling the Philippines without the consent of its people betrayed the principles of the Declaration of Independence. A republic, it said, cannot govern a subject people abroad without giving up the ideals that justify its own existence.

documents.title: Two wars: what annexation cost
documents.source: Figures: Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, "War in the Philippines" (battle deaths); total American deaths 2,446 per U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Filipino deaths are estimates.
documents.sourcing: A table from the course books comparing the Spanish-American War with the war to hold the Philippines. The Spanish-American War cell counts battle deaths (385); total American deaths were 2,446, mostly from disease. The Filipino death toll is an estimate, not an exact count.
documents.text:
| War | Length | American deaths | Filipino deaths |
| Spanish-American War (1898) | 4 months | 385 in battle; 2,446 total | Not counted in the books |
| Philippine-American War (1899-1902) | 3 years | More than 4,000 | 200,000 or more (estimate) |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which debates over imperialism changed American ideas about the nation's role in the world between 1890 and 1902, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the closing of the western frontier, the European scramble for empire, or the Panic of 1893 and the search for markets.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about how the debates changed American ideas.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Treaty of Paris ratification vote of 57 to 27, the Insular Cases of 1901, or the election of 1900.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why the debate split Americans who shared the same ideals, or connecting the annexation debate to later American foreign policy.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The debates over imperialism changed American ideas about the nation's role decisively but not completely: by 1902 Americans accepted that the United States was an overseas power, yet the anti-imperialist claim that empire betrayed republican ideals never went away and shaped how the new empire was defended.
Context: After 1890 the frontier was closing, European powers were carving up Africa and Asia, and the Panic of 1893 left factories searching for markets, so the question of what America should do abroad was suddenly urgent.
Evidence: Documents 1-4 show the expansionist case — Mahan's strategy, Kipling's duty, Beveridge's continuity, McKinley's benevolence. Documents 5-6 show the anti-imperialist answer — Twain's subjugation charge and the League's consent argument. Document 7 shows the price: a three-year war far deadlier than the war against Spain.
Beyond the documents: The Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris 57 to 27, one vote over two-thirds, and the Insular Cases of 1901 let the United States rule colonies without full constitutional rights.
Sourcing: Beveridge speaks as a campaigner arguing for empire; McKinley speaks as the president making policy; Twain speaks as a famous author changing his mind in public; Kipling writes as a Briton urging Americans on.
Complexity: The change was real — America kept the colonies — but the debate's losers set the terms: every defense of empire after 1902 had to answer the charge that it betrayed the republic.
